transcript: Chapter Two, What the Distance Showed Them. They were on the road before first light, and it did not help at all, because the four of them had gone north, and Callie was going north, and at the middle of the morning she came around the shoulder of a cut, and there they were, drawn up and waiting a quarter mile ahead. She stopped the barrow in the road. Don't, her mother said without opening her eyes. I'm not doing anything, you're doing the thing where you look at the ditch. I'm looking at the road. Callie. Callie looked at the ditch. It was a good ditch. It ran about 200 paces along the eastern side, and it was deep enough to put a barrow in, and there was thorn scrub at the far end of it. And she had worked all of that out in something under three seconds, and her mother had known she was doing it from flat on her back with her eyes shut. They picked this on purpose, her mother said. Look where they've stopped. Callie looked. They had stopped in the worst possible place for an ambush, and the best possible place to be seen from. The road ran straight and open for that whole quarter mile with the cut wall on one side and the flat on the other, and the wagon was drawn up square across it with the canvas rolled back, and the team was out of the traces and hobbled, a mule and a horse, which was a thing Callie had never seen anybody do on purpose, and all four people were sitting on the ground on the near side of the wagon where Callie could count them from where she stood. There was a fire. There was a pot on it. There was nowhere for a fifth person to be hiding within 400 paces, and they had arranged it so that this was obvious. That's manners, her mother said. That's somebody with manners. That's somebody who wants something. Those aren't different. Her mother got an elbow under herself and sat up, slowly in stages, and Callie pretended to be busy with the strapping. Go on. Walk it in. And Callie, let them talk first. You've got a terrible habit of filling a silence. I don't fill silences. You're filling one now. At 200 paces, one of them stood up. The big one. He was the biggest person Callie had ever seen stand up. And he did it in a hurry and then plainly did not know what to do with himself. And he lifted one hand about chest high and then thought better of it and put it down, and then lifted it again. She decided on the spot that he was not the problem. At 100 paces, a woman with a bow across her back said something Callie could not hear. And a small dark woman sitting by the fire said something back without turning her head. And the big one sat down again. At 30 paces, Callie stopped the barrow and set the legs down and unclipped the strapping off her chest because she was not going to have a conversation with two lengths of cargo webbing crossed over her ribs. And because she wanted her arms. That's far enough for us, the small dark woman said. Come the rest of it if you want. Stay there if you'd rather. I'd rather here. Then here, the woman stood. She did it without pushing off anything, straight up out of a cross-legged sit. And Callie noticed that and filed it. My name is Katori. That's Pell who drives. Enos who shoots. Otto who lifts. Callie. Callie. Katori said. She was maybe 35. She was a head shorter than Callie's mother, and she stood the way a fence post stands. She had a gray knitted cap pushed back off her forehead, and a flat, unhurried face. And she looked at Callie the way Callie had looked at the sprung snare. We watched you last night. All four of us. For about half an hour. I want that said out loud before anything else. Because you saw us and you'll have been chewing on it since. And I'd rather you chewed on the true version. Callie said nothing. That's the other half of manners, her mother said from the Barrow pleasantly. Tilda. I'd get up. But I'm enjoying myself. Pell laughed. A dry, one-note thing like a latch. He was 60-odd gray to the ears sitting on an upturned crate with a book open on his knee and a pencil stub going behind it. There it is, he said. First civil word out of anybody this morning. Katori, take a note. Pell, taking a note is all I do. Tell me what you saw, Callie said. Katori's eyebrows went up about a sixteenth of an inch. Fair enough. You want to know whether we're worth talking to? I want to know what you saw. A girl came up the drainage about an hour before dark with a hook on her shoulder and went straight to the culvert without slowing down, which told me she'd decided on it from somewhere back. She spent a while at the mouth of it on her hands and knees and we couldn't see what she was doing. Katori's eyes went across Callie's face without any hurry. That's the part I want. Not the killing everybody on this road can kill something once. What was the ten minutes? Callie thought about lying and then thought about what lying would buy her. I cut a step in the silt so I'd have a back foot, she said. I put my coat on the rebar in the crown so I'd know where it was without looking. I paced the gap between the wall and where a big one would stand, because that's how I was coming out. Nobody said anything for a moment. There, said Katori. She got the arm off in the mouth of the culvert, said Ines. She had not moved from where she sat and she had not put the bow down, and she spoke the way she probably did everything, which was without any part left over. Ninety paces, maybe ninety-five. Then she came out through the gap and took it on the open ground going the other way. You could see that from the grade. I could see it from the grade. It was dark. It was not dark yet, said Ines. It was eleven minutes before dark, and I'd already said so twice. She had, said Otto. He had an enormous careful voice, like somebody carrying a full cup. She kept saying it. She says times like that. Eleven minutes, nine minutes. Nobody knows how. I know how, said Ines. Nobody else knows how. We're going to Meridian, Katori said. We've come up from the Warren country in the southeast, which is a long way from here and looks nothing like here. We have freight, and I'd rather not say what, and you'd rather not know. Pell. Pell turned the book around without getting up. It was not a ledger. It was a road atlas, a real pre-fall one, printed in four colors on paper, gone the shade of weak tea, and somebody had been writing over the top of it in pencil for a long time in a small, neat hand. That's us, Pell said, tapping. That's the rail grade you saw us on. And that, he moved the pencil an inch north and stopped it on a long, blue shape with a pale line drawn across the waist of it, is where our information ends and our guessing starts. Because the book says there's a reservoir there with a two-mile causeway over the middle of it. And the book was printed in a year when everything worked. And the book does not know about any of the last sixty years. Callie looked at the page. She had never seen the flats drawn before. It was a strange, cold feeling to see a place she had walked as a shape somebody had made a decision about. The reservoir's down, she said. It's been down since before I was born. There's about a foot of water in the north arm and a wet spring and nothing anywhere else. And the causeway? Standing. The deck's gone off the middle span and somebody laid rail iron across it, and it's held for eleven years that I know of. Pell wrote it down. Will it take a wagon? Katori said. It'll take a wagon. It won't take a wagon and anything coming the other way, because it's one wide and there's no turning on it. Callie stopped. She had not meant to give them that much, and it had come out anyway. And she understood, a beat too late, that this was exactly what her mother had meant about silences. That's free, she said. I'm not selling you that. No, Katori agreed. You're not. You just did. So here it is, Katori said. I'll say it plain and then you can take a while. I want to hire you to Meridian. Two things. You walk the road ahead of us and you tell us what you told me just then, every day, before we get to it instead of after. And when something comes at this wagon, you stand at the back of it with that hook and you do what you did last night. She held up one finger. That's the whole job. I'm not hiring a soldier and I don't want one. I have three people who can hold a line. I do not have one who can look at a bent thistle and tell me where a husk line runs. She's thirteen, said Innes. She is. You watched her fight a husk in a hole in the ground with a farm tool. I did. Katori. Innes. Say the rest of it. Innes was quiet for a second. Then she said flatly. The rest of it is that I couldn't have done it and I'd have got her trying. And I've been telling you since the warren that we needed somebody who knows the ground. There's the rest of it, said Katori. I still don't like it. You're not required to. The crate Pell was sitting on had a lid nailed down in a bad corner. And while the rest of it was going on, he had got off it and got a bar under the lid and was working at it without much success, he made a noise of complaint. Katori put her hand out, palm down, over the crate, and did not look away from Callie while she did it. There was a blade in her hand. Callie had been looking directly at the hand, and she could not have said where the thing came from. It was gray and about the length of a forearm. And it came up out of Katori's closed fist with no more ceremony than a man taking a knife out of a boot, except that it had not been anywhere. Katori put the point in under the lid, once, and leaned. And the nails came out of the wood with a squeal. Then her hand was empty again. There was a flat gray slab in it, about the size of her palm, three fingers thick, rounded at the corners. She turned it over once and put it in her coat. Thank you, said Pell, and went back to his book, and nobody else so much as looked up. Callie became aware that she had not breathed in a while. You've seen an ember, Katori said. It was not really a question. I've seen one off a man at Gaunt's reach. He wore it on a cord, and he showed it to everybody, and he couldn't do anything with it. Hmm. Katori's mouth moved very slightly. That's most of them. Can I ask? You can ask anything. I'll tell you whether I'm answering. Callie found she did not actually have the question yet. It was too big, and it had no edges on it, and it was the same shapeless thing she had been carrying around for two months and had not said out loud to anybody, including her mother. How much of that can you do? She said finally. One shape, said Katori. That shape. I've had it eleven years, and it's one shape, and it does that, and on a bad day it doesn't do that either. She said it without any weight on it at all, the way you'd report the weather. That's what it is. It's a tool that lives in your chest instead of your belt. Anybody who tells you it's more than that is selling you a cord to wear it on. The pay took less time than the argument had. Coins no good to you, and I haven't much, Katori said. So, food off the wagon, both of you, same as the rest of us eat. A tenth share of whatever ash we take between here and Meridian, and I'll not weigh it short, and Pell writes it down so you can look at the number. And I'll stand for you at the Meridian Gate, which is worth more than the other two together, and you should make me say that out loud. Say it out loud. That's worth more than the other two together, Katori said. They don't let people in. They let in people somebody vouched for. Callie looked past her at the wagon. It was a flatbed with hoops over it, and the canvas was rolled back, and the bed was two-thirds full of crates lashed under a net, and the front third of it was bedding and sacks and nothing that mattered. I want the wagon, she said. Pell's pencil stopped. Go on, said Katori. Not the whole wagon. That third, Callie pointed. My mother rides. Not when it's bad. Every day, all day, whether it's bad or not, and nobody gets to have a face about it on the days it isn't. Behind her on the barrow, her mother said, Callie, you're not in this part. I am absolutely in this part. You're not, Callie said, and did not turn around, and kept her eyes on Katori, and found it took everything she had. Katori looked past her at the barrow for a moment. She looked at it for longer than she needed to, and her face did not change, and something behind the face did. Callie saw it go through, the way you see wind cross a field of wheat from a long way off and never see the wind. Done, Katori said. You didn't ask what's wrong with her? No, said Katori. People ask. I know what people do. She turned and started for the mules and stopped, and said, without turning around, Pell will want your terms in the book. Say them to him the way you said them to me. Don't help him by making them smaller. Nine miles, said Pell. What? You were about to ask me what we make in a day, so I'm telling you first to spare us both. Nine miles. Ten on a good road with the load lighter than it is. He licked the pencil, which was a disgusting habit, and wrote, What do you make? Eleven. Twelve, if she's walking. Then you've just bought yourself some days, Pell said, and you knew that when you said it, and I'd like it noted that I noticed. Noted. It's noted. He looked up at her over the top of the atlas. He had the pale, water-colored eyes that very old men on the road sometimes had, and he was not unkind, and he was also not going to pretend at anything. I've been keeping this book eleven years, and it'll tell you every mile and every ounce and what we paid for it. The one thing it doesn't have a column for is what a thing's worth. You'll want to work that out for yourself before the gate. Meridian has columns. They got the barrow up on the wagon bed and lashed, and Otto did it in one movement with the load still in it, which Callie decided not to have feelings about. Her mother went up on the boards with a blanket rolled behind her, and an expression of enormous suffering that fooled nobody and was not meant to. This is undignified, she announced. Yes. I want that understood. I'm going along with it under protest. Understood. Also, there's a crate digging into me. That's the corner of the world, said Otto, very seriously, digging in. And then went red, and went to see to the team. Callie watched him back them in. The mule went into the traces the way a door shuts. The horse went in sideways, in four separate attempts, with her ears going the whole time like something signaling across a valley. Her name's Duchess, Otto said. Her name is nothing, said Pell from the board. You don't name what you might have to eat, and you don't name what's going to put you in a ditch. And she is both. And I've said so since the warren. She's not going to put anybody in a ditch. She's a horse. Pell said it the way another man would have said a number. That's not an insult. It's a specification. A mule will look at a bad thing and stop and stand there and refuse you all afternoon, and you can hit it and it'll go on refusing you. And that refusing has saved my life twice. A horse looks at a bad thing and leaves. That's all a horse is. It's 400 kilos of leaving, and the only question is what's standing where it decides to leave through. You like her. I like her enormously, Pell said. That's a separate column. Callie walked. She walked out ahead of the traces where Katori put her. 30 or 40 paces up, close enough to be shouted to and far enough to be useful, and she found within the first mile that she had no idea what to do with her hands. She had pulled something every day since the spring. Her chest ached where the strapping wasn't. Katori came up alongside her a little before noon and walked with her for a while without saying anything, which Callie was beginning to understand was a thing Katori did on purpose. How old are you? She said eventually. 13. When? The end of the spring. Katori walked another dozen paces. So it hasn't happened. Callie's mouth went dry, which annoyed her. No. Anybody in your town do the words over you? There wasn't anybody left in my town to do the words over anybody. Hmm, said Katori. Does that matter? The words? No, said Katori. Not one bit. But it's better to have somewhere to be. She walked on ahead, and Callie stood for a second in the middle of the road with the flat gray country going north in front of her, and then went after her, and did not ask the next question. Because she had a strong sense that the answer to it was waiting for her somewhere up the road, regardless of whether she asked.
